With Marquis, it locates the wrong of killing in the deprivation of a future-like-ours — a future of valuable experiences, projects, and enjoyments — and observes that the fetus has exactly such a future, owed to the deprivation itself rather than to any present status. entries.title: The objection challenges the burden's direction. A pregnancy, it says, is not a purely private matter on the order of a haircut or a career change: it involves a developing human life, a second party whose stake is the gravest possible. Given that, the default cannot run in favor of termination-on-request. The presumption must favor continuation — the pregnant person who would end the pregnancy bears the burden of justification, not the party who would see it preserved. To treat "her body, her call" as the starting point is to beg the question against the second party by assuming away its standing before the argument has begun. The right placement of the burden is on the chooser to show why the pregnancy may be ended, not on the objector to show why it may not.

entries.title: The objection turns on a disanalogy the bodily-sovereignty default is said to ignore. Thomson's hostage was kidnapped — wired to the violinist without lifting a finger — whereas the pregnant person, in the ordinary case, voluntarily performed the very act that brings the dependent into being, knowing pregnancy to be its foreseeable result. One who knowingly undertakes an action that creates a dependent, the objection runs, assumes responsibility for that dependent, and assumed responsibilities ground duties. The fetus, moreover, exists only because of her act and depends on her body alone; she has created not merely a need but an exclusive need, and to walk away is not the mere declining of aid a stranger may decline but the abandonment of a dependent one has made. So the bodily-sovereignty default is defeated for the ordinary case: voluntary responsibility converts what would otherwise be a permissible withdrawal into a forbidden one, and the analogy to refusing a kidney one never undertook to provide simply does not reach her.

entries.title: The moment the suite asserts a positive moral appraisal of abortion — not merely the right to it, but that abortion wrongs no one and that antinatalism supplies a reason in its favor — it steps onto the slope toward judging which lives are worth living. The positive reason offered is harm-prevention: abortion spares a would-be person the guaranteed harms of existence. But harm is not uniform. A pregnancy carrying a severe, foreseeable burden of suffering would, on the suite's own logic, give a stronger reason for termination than an ordinary one — and now the suite grades lives by their projected harm-load, leaning hardest against the lives that would suffer most. That is the structure of eugenics: the ranking of existences by worth, the marking of some lives as better never lived. The non-comparative label the suite attaches does not save it — one may grant that the consideration applies to every conception and still note that it applies with graded force, and the gradient is the selection. The appraisal cannot stay universal once its own reason admits of degree.

entries.title: The objection concedes the ground already taken — that bodies are not conscriptable, that voluntary sex grounds no duty to gestate — and resists at the one point those concessions leave open: the manner of the act. Bodily sovereignty, on Thomson's own analysis, licenses withdrawing the use of one's body. You unplug yourself from the violinist and he dies, but of his own kidney ailment, not your hand; you have declined to go on serving as his life-support, which is your right, and his pre-existing condition does the rest. Abortion, the objection presses, is frequently nothing so passive. To dismember a fetus, or to induce its demise before removal, is not to cease lending a body but to actively end a life — and the right not to sustain another is not a right to kill him. The killing/letting-die distinction is a weighty moral primitive: you may unplug the violinist, you may not reach over and stab him, though he dies either way. So even granting the bodily-sovereignty default in full, the objection concludes, the manner of abortion forfeits the right wherever it crosses from withdrawing support into actively killing the dependent — a line the violinist analogy draws and most abortions cross.

entries.title: The objection insists the entire question turns on a single metaphysical fact: the moral status of the fetus. Whether abortion may be chosen, it says, depends wholly on whether the fetus is a person. If it is a person, then ending the pregnancy ends a person's life, and no consideration drawn from the pregnant person's body can convert a homicide into a permissible act — the right collapses into a license to kill. If it is not a person, the right is genuine but empty, a permission opposed by no one and needing no defense. Either way, the objection presses, the personhood question is dispositive, and a defense that will not answer it has skipped the one step on which everything depends. A suite that routes around fetal status, in this telling, has not defended the right; it has changed the subject.

entries.title: > "Set every argument aside. What actually moves you to deny humanity any special standing is not the weakness of the grounds — it is animus: contempt for your own kind, dressed in the language of unproven mandates and absent capacities. A stance powered by hatred of humanity is not one you are *permitted* to hold as a serious moral position; it is self-harm in the costume of philosophy, and it disqualifies itself. Grant that every ground-argument failed — your dissent still stands convicted by its motive. You do not withhold because the case is thin; you withhold because you despise what you are, and you would not lift a finger to keep the species in the world. (Or, more gently: you do not really *lack* the human-intuition every human shares. You are posturing. Either way the refusal is not in good standing.)"

entries.title: > "Concede the parity gap whole — I won't smuggle a threshold, and I won't draw the line at the species border, because you've shown no genuine capacity falls there. But you assumed I needed a line at all. Drop the threshold framing: standing is not a badge you clear a bar to wear, it is a *magnitude*, and the magnitude tracks capacity. Humans, on average, have more of what grounds standing — more rational agency, richer self-awareness, deeper temporal extension — and so, on average, more standing. The marginal cases stop being counterexamples and become confirmations: the profoundly impaired human has proportionally less, the exceptional animal proportionally more, exactly as a gradient predicts. I bite that without a wince. There is no line for you to break because I have drawn none — only a slope, and on the slope humans simply rank highest. The gradient is honest where the line was crude."

entries.title: Anthropocentrism is the **default**. It is woven into language (we say "person" and mean human; "humane" is a compliment), into law (rights attach to humans as such), into practice, and into pre-reflective intuition. A position that pervasive and that load-bearing does not stand in need of a defense — it *is* the resting state of reasoning about moral standing. The dissenter is the one making the **extraordinary claim**: that humanity's privileged standing should be revoked or suspended. Extraordinary claims carry the burden of proof. So the dissenter, not the anthropocentrist, owes an argument. And until that positive argument for de-privileging humanity is actually **discharged**, human-centrism stands as the *rational* default — and dissent from it, having produced no such argument, is **arbitrary, perverse, even irrational**: a departure from the settled with nothing to show for it.

entries.title: > "Concede the burden is symmetric — I won't lean on the default. Here is the ground. Humans possess capacity **C**: rational agency, the capacity to give and demand reasons, to enter reciprocal justification, to hold oneself answerable to norms — name it as you like, it is real and it is morally weighty. And the marginal cases don't embarrass it: a kind is characterized by its mature, typical form, not by its damaged exceptions. So the privilege is not arbitrary incumbency — it *tracks* C. Anthropocentrism is just the recognition that bearers of C are owed a standing the C-less are not, and humans are the bearers of C." This is the privilege the anti-mandate node (`human-centrism-is-the-default`) explicitly declined to engage and handed forward: the spine defeats the privilege only while it is *bare*; the moment a ground is named, the dispute moves here. The objection has pre-loaded its best defense (the kind-norm rescue) into the first statement. Good — it gets met.

But you assumed the ground had to be a *capacity*. It needn't be. Membership in the human kind — the human form of life — is *itself* the morally relevant fact, not derivatively through any capacity. It is **the kind that matters** (Cohen); the marginal human has standing *qua* member. And the demand for a *species-neutral* justification of human partiality is confused (Williams): it asks me to occupy a 'point of view of the universe' from which the very notion of what-matters loses its grip. **'They're human, like us' is already a complete reason.** Calling it 'prejudice' begs the question — it assumes species is morally idle the way race is, which is precisely what's in dispute. There is nothing here for you to refute, and no neutral tribunal you can summon me to."

I am resting it on what a thing is made of and as: a living, biological organism. Standing-bearing properties — a point of view, interests, the capacity to be wronged — can inhere only in that kind of substrate. A silicon system, however fluently it behaves, is the wrong sort of thing for them to inhere in. So the non-biological case is not a *member* whose standing I am denying. It is a category to which standing-talk does not reach — and your readiness to extend standing to it is not generosity, it is a category mistake."

entries.title: Set aside whether the suffering will lift — grant that it won't, or that no one can know. Death is still the one choice you cannot revise. Every other decision leaves a standing self who can reconsider, adapt, be surprised by a future they couldn't foresee; death forecloses the chooser along with the choice. When one branch is irreversible and the other is not, and you are deciding under uncertainty, the precautionary structure of the situation — not optimism, not the prognosis — favors the branch that keeps every option open. Even a competent, settled agent should defer to that asymmetry, and a regime that lets the irreversible branch be taken has failed to respect it. Better the error you can still walk back.

The wrong is not that you destroy something valuable; it is that the maxim instrumentalizes your own rational nature, the very thing whose dignity grounds all value in the first place. So it holds even if life itself is worth nothing: the prohibition rides on the form of the willing, not the worth of the life, and no degree of misery exempts you from a duty you owe your own personhood.

entries.title: Medicine runs on scarcity — a finite stock of palliative beds, clinician hours, hospice capacity, and end-of-life funding, allocated against more need than there is supply. A legal assisted-death program does not draw on some separate reserve; it draws on that same stock. Every assessment, every provision, every clinician trained and hour spent staffing the regime is capacity not spent on a patient who wanted to live and could have been helped. That is harm to others in the plainest form — not a message, not an imitation, but a bed a third party needed and did not get. Mill's principle licenses restricting a liberty that harms others; here the harm is direct, the resource is finite, and someone goes without. Where the diversion is genuinely net-negative for the system and no narrower fix is on offer, the harm-to-others is real and unanswered — and it licenses foreclosing the option.

entries.title: A right to transition presupposes that the person validly consents to the interventions it covers, and valid consent requires decision-making capacity. But gender dysphoria is, by its own clinical description, a state of acute and sometimes severe psychological distress, and a person in the grip of such distress cannot weigh a decision of this magnitude soundly. Acute distress narrows attention, biases judgment toward relief, and impairs the dispassionate weighing of long-term consequences that competent consent demands — and the more the distress bears on the very thing being decided, the more it distorts the deciding, as a phobia distorts judgment of its object. So the consent on which the right rests is given from a state that defeats the capacity valid consent requires — and absent capacitated consent, there is no autonomous choice for the right to protect.

But the desire to transition is, in a growing number of cases, socially induced rather than the person's own: it spreads through peer clusters, online communities, and social media in patterns that look contagious — rapid, imitative, sharply clustered onset, often in cohorts with no prior history. A desire produced this way is not authentically the person's own; it is something caught from a social environment. Consent rooted in an induced desire is not voluntary in the sense valid consent requires, and an involuntary consent is no consent at all. So the right rests on a choice that is not, in these cases, freely the chooser's own — and absent a voluntary choice, there is no autonomous decision for the right to protect.

entries.title: A right to transition presupposes that the interventions it covers are the kind of thing a person may be left free to choose, and a choice that predictably ruins a substantial fraction of those who make it is not. Transition is such a choice. A significant share of those who transition come to regret it and detransition, often after changes that cannot be undone — sterility, surgically altered bodies, the lasting marks of cross-sex hormones — so that the regret, when it comes, falls on a person who can no longer return to what they were. This is not the ordinary risk attending any serious decision; it is grave, irreversible harm visited on the very people the right is meant to serve, at a rate no responsible practice would accept for an elective intervention. A liberty whose exercise inflicts harm of this severity on so many of those who exercise it does not earn protection as a right — the harm to the chooser is real enough, and common enough, to override the liberty interest, and the responsible course is to foreclose the option or hedge it with restrictions stringent enough that the harm is prevented rather than merely regretted.

entries.title: A right to transition does not stay self-regarding. Exercising it places trans women in sex-segregated sport, changing rooms, shelters, and prison wings, and that imposes real costs on cis women and girls who have competing claims of their own. The bodily advantages of a male-typical puberty — mass, skeletal frame, cardiovascular ceiling — are not erased by transition, making the female sports category unfair and, in contact sport, unsafe: cis competitors are displaced from podiums, records, and scholarships. And in single-sex provision for vulnerable women — domestic-violence shelters, women's prisons — inclusion can compromise privacy, dignity, or safety, against populations least able to absorb the cost. These are third parties with their own claims to fair competition, bodily privacy, and single-sex provision; the right reaches past the self and lands on them. A permission that harms others cannot be the modest, self-regarding thing it advertises.

entries.title: The objection turns the suite's own Firewall against it. The charter forbids the suite from exhorting transition, from resting on a dysphoria-relief or any suffering-reduction premise, and from deploying a Benatar-style asymmetry. Yet a defense that systematically defeats every objection to transition cannot help but FUNCTION as advocacy: the cumulative brief makes the choice look unassailable, which is exhortation by other means. Worse, the defense must covertly rest on the merits it disclaims, for one defends a right to do X only because one judges X worth doing, so a suppressed dysphoria-relief premise is doing the real work; and the harm strand's signature move, concede the harm and defend the right to bear it, can only succeed if the foreclosure-harm silently outweighs the intervention-harm, a hidden asymmetry, a suffering-calculus in disguise. If any of this lands, the Firewall is a fiction, the expressivist and Benatar objections become true at the charter level, and the entire optionality framing is self-refuting.

entries.title: A right to transition presupposes that the person can give valid informed consent to the interventions it covers — cross-sex hormones, surgeries. Valid informed consent requires adequate information about consequences; but here the evidence base is thin and the long-term effects are genuinely uncertain — the durability of benefits, the rates and reversibility of harms, the effects on fertility, bone density, and cardiovascular and cognitive function over decades are not well established. A competent adult cannot give informed consent to interventions whose consequences are unknown: that is a leap in the dark dressed as autonomy, not informed consent. So the right rests on a consent that cannot in fact be given — and absent valid consent, there is no autonomous choice for the right to protect.

The combine that brings in the soy and wheat minces field mice, voles, ground-nesting birds, rabbits by the million; pesticide poisons more; clearing habitat for monocrop starves out whole populations. My one forgone purchase is swallowed by the buffer - expected animals spared, near enough to zero to call it zero. A duty to perform an act that changes nothing is no duty. So grant that your ethics is flawless: it still lands on no one. It cannot reach me.

entries.title: Plants are alive too — and don't tell me they don't feel it. Cut one and it floods the wound with chemicals; wound another and it signals its neighbours to arm up; Gagliano's peas even learned to expect a fan like Pavlov's dog. Electrical signalling runs the whole organism. So how are you so sure the wheat feels nothing while the pig feels everything? Draw the line honestly and you can't — 'animals in, plants out' is just a preference for creatures that look back at you. Either your suffering rule is arbitrary, or it convicts your salad too: every plate is a killing floor, and the only consistent vegan is a corpse. So climb down off the high ground — you eat the living, same as me.
